verified_facts.fact: Google published this on 2026-09-17; the post's byline date line reads 'Sep 17, 2026' and the author is Tom Shane, Senior Product Manager, Google Labs.
The standfirst states what changed: an experimental agent built for families, aimed at reducing household logistics.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Google Labs introduces a new experimental agent built for families, helping households spend less time on logistics and more time together.

verified_facts.fact: CC is not new on this date. Google states it launched CC as a personal agent, that it became a daily habit for early testers, and that in May it was brought to the Gemini app as Daily Brief.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: It quickly became a daily habit for many early testers and in May we brought it to the Gemini App as Daily Brief .

verified_facts.fact: THE CORE CHANGE, in one sentence: CC gets its own Google account, which Google says gives it a distinct identity and a clear permissions model, and up to six members can manage and collaborate with it.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: It has its own Google account that gives CC a distinct identity and clear permissions model, enabling up to six members to manage and collaborate with the agent.

verified_facts.fact: The sharing boundary Google states: CC only sees what each member chooses to share, and Google's examples are emails from a child's school, a local swim centre or the vet.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: CC only sees what each member chooses to share, such as emails from your child’s school, the local swim center, or the vet.

verified_facts.fact: The account is described as verified, and Google states two limits on it: it only responds to group members, and it will not act or share outside the group without permission.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: It only responds to group members, and will not take action or share information outside the group without your permission.

verified_facts.fact: Feature 1, the shared morning brief: each morning CC delivers a shared 'Your Day Ahead' brief covering who needs to be where, what needs doing, and what CC completed the previous day.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Each morning, CC delivers a shared “Your Day Ahead” brief.

verified_facts.fact: Feature 2: CC tracks dates and to-dos and pulls shared information into a family Calendar or Task list, keeping them up to date as things change.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: CC automatically tracks important dates and to-dos, pulling relevant shared information from across your group into a family Calendar or Task list, and helps keep them up to date even as things change.

verified_facts.fact: Feature 3, and the one that involves CC acting rather than summarising: filling out permission slips or activity registration PDFs, creating school supply shopping lists, and drafting weekly meal plans. Google says CC will ask for missing details and update its group memory.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: such as filling out permission slips or activity registration PDFs, creating school supply shopping lists, or crafting weekly meal plans

verified_facts.fact: Google states the permission condition for that acting, in an image caption under the feature.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: CC can take action, like filling out forms, with your permission.

verified_facts.fact: Control 1 - per-member sharing: each member chooses what to share and what to keep private, and can change it at any time.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Each member can easily choose what to share with CC and what to keep private, and can make changes at any time.

verified_facts.fact: Control 2 - standing rules by sender: a member can pick email senders that are always shared with CC going forward, and receives a private weekly list of new senders to choose from.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Pick the email senders that you always want to share with CC going forward, like your kids’ school or travel bookings. Each week, you’ll also receive a private list of new email senders that you can choose to share with CC.

verified_facts.fact: Control 3 - one-off sharing: a member can forward something to CC by email or Google Chat, including a photo of an invitation, or share a Drive folder or files with it, or add CC to a Calendar.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: You can also share a Drive folder or files with CC or add CC to a Calendar.

verified_facts.fact: What CC connects to, and what it runs on: Gmail, Chat, Docs and Calendar; every CC runs on its own isolated cloud computer powered by Google's agentic harness Antigravity and the latest Gemini models.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Behind the scenes, every CC runs on its own isolated cloud computer powered by Google’s agentic harness, Antigravity , and the latest Gemini models.

verified_facts.fact: Google names a concrete capability that reaches outside Google's own apps: checking live drive times from the Google Maps API between back-to-back activities.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: checking live drive times from the Google Maps API between back-to-back activities

verified_facts.fact: Memory is split between household and individual. Google's own examples: a go-to grocery list or favourite family restaurants for the household; dietary preferences or local timezones for one person.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: CC remembers what applies to the whole household (like your go-to grocery list or favorite family restaurants) versus what belongs to one person (like dietary preferences or local timezones).

verified_facts.fact: AVAILABILITY, the single most restrictive sentence in the post, quoted with Google's own missing period after 'U.S': an early Labs experiment, web and mobile, people 18 or over, in the U.S, with a personal Google account.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: CC is an early experiment from Google Labs, available on web and mobile for people (18+) in the U.S with a personal Google account.

verified_facts.fact: Two different entry paths, and neither is immediate: existing users are told they will receive an upgrade email 'in the coming days', while new users join a waitlist.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Existing users will receive an email in the coming days to upgrade their account and new users can join the waitlist .

verified_facts.fact: CC's original launch is dated Dec 16, 2025 on Google's own earlier post, and it was described then as a personal productivity agent built with Gemini that connects Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive and the wider web.
The original CC delivered the same 'Your Day Ahead' briefing, but to one person's inbox each morning - which is exactly what the 2026-09-17 change turns into a shared brief.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: delivering a “Your Day Ahead” briefing to your inbox every morning

verified_facts.fact: THE TWO AVAILABILITY SENTENCES DO NOT MATCH, and both are Google's. The December 2025 post says early access in the U.S. AND CANADA, 18+, 'starting with Google AI Ultra and paid subscribers'. The September 2026 post says the U.S only, 18+, 'with a personal Google account', and names no subscription at all.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: CC is an early Labs experiment, launching in early access today to Google consumer account users 18+ in the U.S. and Canada, starting with Google AI Ultra and paid subscribers.

verified_facts.fact: Daily Brief, the Gemini-app form of CC that the post points to, carries its own rollout limit on Google's product page: eligible users in select regions, with more users, languages and countries promised only as a hope.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Daily Brief is currently rolling out to eligible users in select regions.

verified_facts.fact: Google describes what Daily Brief does in the Gemini app, which is the narrower thing a reader outside the U.S. might actually be able to reach: scanning inbox, calendar and tasks and serving a prioritised morning summary.
verified_facts.verbatim_quote: Allow Gemini to dig through your digital clutter and scan your inbox, calendar, and tasks at hand.

No language scope. The post names no interface language, and does not say whether CC works in Traditional Chinese or any language other than English.
No date for the upgrade emails beyond 'in the coming days', and no waitlist length, no acceptance criteria and no estimate of how long a waitlist entry takes.

No statement about children. The product is described as being for families and the examples are school forms and children's activities, but the eligibility line is 18+ - so a child cannot be one of the six members by Google's own rule. Google does not address this tension anywhere on the page.

Google says CC only sees what is shared and will not act outside the group without permission, but the post does not say where the shared email content is stored, how long it is kept, whether it is used to improve Google's models, or how a member removes what they previously shared.
No statement about what happens when a member leaves the group, when the shared memory is deleted, or who owns CC's Google account.

No accuracy or error information: no statement about what happens if CC fills a registration form wrongly, books the wrong time, or misreads an email, and no way described to review an action before it is taken beyond the general 'with your permission'.
No usage limits, quotas or caps of any kind.
No independent testing. Every capability in this record is Google's description of its own product; this site has run no test.
No explanation of what Antigravity is beyond the phrase 'Google's agentic harness', and no link between it and any model version number - 'the latest Gemini models' is not a version.

editorial_brief:
READER AND ANGLE. Written for a Taiwanese general reader who runs a household - school notices in one person's inbox, a clinic reminder in another's, a group chat that nobody reads back. The reader cannot use CC; it is US-only. The article is worth their time anyway because it is the clearest published example so far of a design question that will reach them: when an assistant serves several people at once, whose information does it hold, and who decides? Google's answer is unusually concrete - give the agent its own account, cap the group at six, and make every person decide sender by sender what it may read.

THE CENTRAL FACT TO GET RIGHT. Google names exactly one country, the U.S., and names it in a sentence that also carries 18+, web and mobile, and a personal Google account. Write that as Google's stated availability, then stop - no prediction about Taiwan in either direction, because Google publishes no roadmap for the family version. The second is the subscription question: Google's December 2025 post said Google AI Ultra and paid subscribers, the September 2026 post says a personal Google account, and Google never says the requirement changed. Report both with dates; do not resolve it.

WHAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN A PRODUCT NOTE. Three details carry the piece. The agent has its own verified Google account, so it appears in a thread the way a person does. Sharing is per member and per sender, with a private weekly list of new senders to approve - a standing rule, not a one-off grant. And the memory is deliberately split between what belongs to the household and what belongs to one person. Those are three answers to 'how do you share an assistant without sharing your inbox', and a reader can judge them without ever installing anything.

SUGGESTED FIVE SECTIONS. (1) What Google announced (its post prints Sep 17, 2026; 18 September Taipei time), and that CC is not new - it launched in December 2025 and became Daily Brief in the Gemini app in May. (2) The three things it does for a household - shared morning brief, shared calendar and tasks, filling forms and lists - ending with the required table (max 4 columns: 功能 / 誰能用 / 需要誰同意 / 官方未說明的部分; 4-6 rows; caption dated 2026-09-18). (3) The design question: an agent with its own account, a six-member cap, per-member and per-sender sharing, and a memory split between household and individual; diagram goes here. (4) The conditions a reader must not skip: the U.S., 18+, a waitlist or an email 'in the coming days', and the unresolved subscription question - plus the 18+ rule sitting oddly inside a family product, stated as a tension Google does not address. (5) What Google did not say - storage, retention, training use, what happens when a member leaves, what happens when the agent fills a form wrongly - and what the Gemini app's Daily Brief offers instead, with its own 'select regions' limit.

ORIGINAL SCENARIO, to be labelled as an editorial example per BRIEF. A household where the school notices arrive in one parent's mailbox and the clinic reminders in the other's. The editorial point is that the hard part was never summarising - it is deciding, in advance and per sender, what the shared assistant is allowed to open, and being able to change that later. That is a question a reader can answer for any shared tool they already use.

TONE AND SCOPE. Plain and practical; no enthusiasm about convenience and no alarm about surveillance. Deliberately out of scope: how background agents decide what to automate (covered 2026-05-19); anything from the AI-generated summary panel; any Gemini version number; any comparison with Apple, Amazon or any other household assistant, since Google makes none; any hands-on impression.
